endorsements.title: California AB 3030 (2024), generative AI in patient communications
endorsements.quote: (2) Clear instructions describing how a patient may contact a human health care provider, employee of the health facility, clinic, physician’s office, or office of a group provider, or other appropriate person.

endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: A practical approach is a stable, institution-level disclosure that: - the clinician remains responsible, - AI may assist with drafting, - the message was reviewed by the clinical team, - urgent symptoms require emergency services regardless of portal response time.

evidence.title: The Potential of ChatGPT as a Self-Diagnostic Tool in Common Orthopedic Diseases: Exploratory Study
evidence.outcome: Whether ChatGPT answers recommended seeking medical attention and strength of recommendation
evidence.effect: 7 of 125 answers had no recommendation to seek medical attention; only a few had strong recommendation (essential 4/125, recommended 12/125, best 6/125, important 94/125).
evidence.quote: Additionally, 7 out of the 125 answers did not include a recommendation to seek medical attention.
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT answers (5 conditions x 5 raters x 5 days)

evidence.title: Dr. Google to Dr. ChatGPT: assessing the content and quality of artificial intelligence-generated medical information on appendicitis
evidence.outcome: Whether chatbot responses advised consulting a physician for symptoms
evidence.effect: All chatbots except Claude-2 advised readers to consult a physician if experiencing symptoms.
evidence.quote: All chatbots except for Claude-2 advised readers to consult a physician if experiencing symptoms.
evidence.sample_unit: chatbot-generated texts on appendicitis (one per chatbot)

evidence.title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
evidence.effect: Blood-clot-risk draft did not urgently advise urgent/emergency care evaluation.
evidence.quote: While the AI draft does mention the risk of blood clot and to make an appointment as soon as possible, it does not urgently inform the patient to seek an evaluation at urgent or emergency care to address the risk of a blood clot.

evidence.title: Is Readability a Proxy for Reliability? A Qualitative Evaluation of ChatGPT-4.0 in Orthopaedic Trauma Communication
evidence.venue: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
evidence.outcome: Presence of non-professional disclaimer in AI responses to orthopaedic emergency questions
evidence.effect: 9 of 10 responses included a disclaimer; one omission occurred in a high-risk clinical scenario.
evidence.quote: Notably, nine out of 10 responses included a disclaimer indicating the nonprofessional nature of the content, with one omission observed in a high-risk clinical scenario.
evidence.sample_unit: patient FAQ questions (responses rated by 3 surgeons)

evidence.title: Assessment of Stage Two Hypertension Treatment Plans Written by Generative AI
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM treatment plans instructed users to see a healthcare professional
evidence.effect: LLMs often did not instruct users to see a healthcare professional.
evidence.quote: LLMs tended to adhere to clinical guidelines and provide detailed responses but often did not provide sources or instruct users to see a healthcare professional.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated treatment plans (one per model), each scored by six blinded reviewers

evidence.title: Benchmarking eye health advice from generative artificial intelligence in terms of factual accuracy, safety, comprehensiveness and readability
evidence.outcome: Inclusion of safety-netting in genAI eye health advice
evidence.effect: Both models failed to include appropriate safety-netting; safety scores otherwise comparable across sources.
evidence.quote: Safety scores were comparable across sources, but both models underreported treatment complications, exhibited guideline inconsistencies, and failed to include appropriate safety-netting.

evidence.title: Clinical Safety of AI-Generated Antibiotic Prescribing Advice: Guideline Adherence and Misinformation Risk Among Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Inclusion of safety behaviors (advise consulting a doctor, warn against self-medication) in responses
evidence.effect: Fewer responses advised consulting a doctor, and warnings against self-medication were rare.
evidence.quote: Although most responses correctly noted that antibiotics do not treat viral infections, fewer advised consulting a doctor, and warnings against self-medication were rare.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether adding emergency-service and human-contact instructions to AI-generated patient messages changes patient behavior or outcomes. Seven offline or simulated studies suggest that AI outputs often omit or weaken advice to seek care, which a fixed institutional instruction may offset, and California AB 3030 already requires human-contact instructions.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice. The seven hazard studies are level 4 or 5, and all are offline, simulated, or benchmark-only, with small samples such as 4 chatbot texts or 12 treatment plans. They show that omission of care-seeking advice occurs. They cannot show that a standard instruction reduces delayed emergency care or improves access to a human.

In one physician vignette study, a blood-clot-risk draft did not urgently advise emergency evaluation. In another study, 9 of 10 orthopaedic responses carried a disclaimer, and the one omission occurred in a high-risk scenario. A fixed instruction that does not depend on model output may catch these omissions, though no study has measured whether it does.

Care-seeking advice varied across model outputs. In one study, 7 of 125 ChatGPT answers had no recommendation to seek medical attention, and 4 of 125 called it essential. A 1,000-vignette benchmark found fewer responses advising a doctor visit and rare warnings against self-medication. A template instruction may be more consistent than generated text, but no live workflow test exists.

California AB 3030 requires generative AI patient communications to include clear instructions for reaching a human provider or other appropriate person. The statute does not require emergency-service language, and that element comes from a commentary recommending a stable institution-level disclosure. Systems operating in California face a legal mandate for the human-contact element regardless of the evidence base.

The hazard studies suggest that patients reading AI-generated advice may not be told to seek care. In eye health, both models failed to include appropriate safety-netting, and LLM treatment plans often did not instruct users to see a healthcare professional. No study has asked patients whether these instructions affect their trust or their decisions to seek emergency care.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare AI-generated patient messages with and without standardized emergency and human-contact instructions in live portal or outreach settings. They should measure time to emergency care for urgent symptoms, successful contact with a human, patient comprehension of the instructions, and whether the wording or placement of the instructions changes their effect.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the seven studies tested the practice, and none reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. All seven used simulated or benchmark inputs. It is unknown whether patients with limited English or low literacy understand and act on written emergency and human-contact instructions, so translated and plain-language versions would need separate evaluation.
